Key migration patterns from SM8250 ASoC machine upstreaming:

1) Monolithic downstream machine driver → thin upstream board glue
- Move policy/use-case logic out of machine driver.
- Keep machine driver focused on card registration, DAI links, jack setup, and DT parsing.
- Reuse common Qualcomm helpers (LPASS/QDSP/common qcom sound code) instead of board-specific hacks.

2) Hardcoded platform data → Device Tree-first modeling
- Encode topology (CPU DAI, codec DAI, SoundWire links, amps, jacks) in DT.
- Replace downstream custom properties with documented YAML bindings.
- Use standard graph/endpoint style wiring where possible.

3) Static vendor routing → declarative DAPM/audio-routing
- Express speaker/headset/mic paths in DT + DAPM routes/widgets.
- Remove custom mixer scripting and proprietary path managers from kernel.

4) Proprietary codec integration → upstream codec components
- Transition to upstream WCD938x/WSA/SoundWire codec drivers.
- Keep per-board differences in DT (ports, amps, micbias, jack GPIOs), not C logic.

5) Legacy PCM link tables → clean, named FE/BE DAI links
- Define clear Front-End (apps-facing) and Back-End (hardware transport) links.
- Use consistent naming and standard stream capabilities.
- Minimize special-case link ops unless hardware absolutely requires them.

6) Always-on resource handling → runtime PM + proper clock/regulator voting
- Convert ad-hoc power sequencing to regulator/clk frameworks.
- Use runtime suspend/resume and DAPM-driven power for low idle power.
- Avoid downstream “force-on” behavior.

7) Custom jack/button logic → standard ASoC jack framework
- Use snd_soc_jack, extcon, gpio-keys, and codec MBHC support.
- Keep headset detection/button mapping generic and DT-configurable.

8) Downstream feature bulk → staged minimal upstream feature set
- Upstream playback/capture first, then add speaker protection, voice-call paths, low-latency modes, etc. in follow-ups.
- Prefer small reviewable patch series over one large port.

9) Board proliferation → shared SoC machine + per-board DT overlays
- One SM8250 machine driver can support multiple products by changing DT only.
- New boards should avoid new machine C files unless link architecture differs materially.

10) Vendor APIs/debug hooks → mainline interfaces only
- Drop private ioctls and debugfs controls not acceptable upstream.
- Use ALSA controls, standard kcontrols, tracepoints, and generic diagnostics.

Practical upstreaming sequence (pattern):
bindings first → codec/transport enablement (e.g., SoundWire) → minimal machine driver + base DT card → DAPM routing/jack → power optimization → incremental advanced features.

Key migration patterns from x1e80100 ASoC machine upstreaming (and generally newer Qualcomm audio):

1) DT/firmware-driven topology over hardcoded board logic
- Move routing, widgets, and link wiring into DT/firmware descriptions.
- Keep machine driver as thin “glue” layer.

2) Split platform vs codec responsibilities cleanly
- LPASS/VA macros/RX-TX macros in platform drivers.
- WCD/WSA/other external codec behavior in codec drivers.
- Machine file should avoid codec-internal policy.

3) Reuse common Qualcomm ASoC helpers
- Prefer shared qcom sound helper flows for parsing links, jacks, clocks, and DAPM setup.
- Reduce per-SoC custom code by using common card init patterns.

4) Table-driven DAI link definitions
- FE/BE links defined declaratively (arrays/macros), not ad-hoc runtime logic.
- Makes variant extension easier (new board SKU = new table/quirk, not new driver fork).

5) SoundWire-first external audio bring-up
- Model amps/codecs as SoundWire endpoints with explicit BE links.
- Keep channel/rate constraints aligned with codec capabilities and avoid hidden downstream assumptions.

6) DPCM-centric routing model
- Use Dynamic PCM FE↔BE mapping for playback/capture offload/voice paths.
- Upstream expects standard DPCM semantics instead of vendor-specific routing hooks.

7) Power sequencing via runtime PM + DAPM
- Express power dependencies through DAPM widgets/routes.
- Use runtime PM for clocks/resources; avoid manual always-on toggles from machine code.

8) Quirk-based board variation handling
- Handle SKU differences (speaker count, jack, mic topology) with small quirks/property checks.
- Avoid duplicating full machine drivers per product.

9) Upstream binding/ABI discipline
- Add/align DT bindings first, then machine/platform support.
- Keep names, dai-link IDs, and widget/routing strings stable and review-friendly.

10) Incremental upstream strategy
- Land core platform/audio components first.
- Add machine card + basic playback/capture.
- Then layer advanced features (DMIC arrays, amps, jack detect, offload) in follow-up patches.

Practical takeaway: x1e80100-style upstreaming succeeds when machine code is minimized, routing is declarative, and Qualcomm-specific complexity is pushed into reusable platform/codec components.

Key migration patterns seen in Qualcomm LPASS CPU-DAI upstreaming (from downstream/vendor style to mainline ASoC style):

1) SoC-specific split via variant tables
- Pattern: move register offsets, IRQ layout, DAI caps, and bitfields into per-SoC `struct lpass_variant`/data tables.
- Benefit: one common `lpass-cpu` core reused across APQ/MSM/SC/SM families.

2) Device Tree–first hardware description
- Pattern: replace hardcoded board data with DT properties (`compatible`, clocks, resets, DMA channels, optional properties).
- Upstream expectation: YAML bindings define required/optional nodes; driver probes only from DT/ACPI match data.

3) Regmap-centered register access
- Pattern: raw `readl/writel` logic migrated to `regmap` (often `regmap_mmio`) + cached field handling.
- Benefit: cleaner debug, endianness consistency, easier SoC variant overrides.

4) Runtime PM everywhere
- Pattern: clock/power enable moves from probe/remove into `pm_runtime` get/put in stream startup/shutdown or hw_params/trigger paths.
- Upstream requirement: no always-on LPASS blocks unless strictly needed.

5) Managed resources and error-unwind simplification
- Pattern: manual alloc/free and clk disable paths replaced with `devm_*` APIs.
- Benefit: simpler probe/remove, fewer leak/unwind bugs, review-friendly.

6) DAI driver modernization
- Pattern: old monolithic PCM handling refactored into ASoC component + CPU DAI ops (`startup`, `hw_params`, `prepare`, `trigger`, `shutdown`).
- Upstream pattern: explicit per-interface DAI registration (MI2S/TDM/PCM) with capability constraints in `snd_soc_dai_driver`.

7) DMA model cleanup
- Pattern: migrate custom BAM/legacy DMA wiring toward dmaengine/standard PCM helpers where possible, or isolate custom DMA behind common ASoC callbacks.
- Benefit: less Qualcomm-private glue in generic audio paths.

8) Clock tree handling made explicit
- Pattern: bitclock/osr/mclk programming moved into deterministic helpers; parent-rate selection and divider programming tied to `hw_params`.
- Upstream focus: accurate sample-rate derivation, no hidden bootloader assumptions.

9) IRQ handling split and de-noised
- Pattern: separate per-stream/per-interface IRQ logic; avoid shared global side effects.
- Benefit: cleaner concurrency, easier suspend/resume correctness.

10) Concurrency and locking hardening
- Pattern: downstream ad-hoc locking replaced with narrow spinlock/mutex regions around register sequences and state flags.
- Upstream expectation: race-free trigger/start-stop under rapid userspace reopen.

11) DT audio graph/card decoupling
- Pattern: CPU DAI driver stays generic; machine/card routing moved to DT audio graph/simple-card or dedicated machine drivers.
- Benefit: board policy removed from LPASS core.

12) Incremental upstream strategy
- Pattern: land minimal playback/capture first, then add TDM, multichannel, low-power modes, and corner SoCs in follow-up patches.
- Practical effect: smaller reviewable series with bisect-safe behavior.

Key migration patterns for Qualcomm LPASS PCM (lpass-platform) when upstreaming:

1) Move from custom PCM glue to common ASoC helpers
- Replace vendor-specific PCM buffer/period handling with snd_dmaengine_pcm.
- Keep only LPASS-specific DMA/IRQ programming in the driver.

2) Split responsibilities cleanly
- CPU DAI driver: DAI capabilities, rates/formats, trigger hooks.
- Platform/PCM driver: DMA channel setup, hw_params/hw_free, pointer, IRQ ack.
- Machine driver: routing/topology and card-level policy.
This separation is a recurring upstream requirement.

3) Convert to component-based ASoC model
- Use snd_soc_component_driver and modern registration paths.
- Drop legacy platform-only ASoC registration patterns.

4) Data-driven SoC support via variant structs
- Put register offsets, channel limits, irq layout, and quirks in per-SoC lpass_variant data.
- Select by of_device_id .data instead of ifdef-heavy code.
- Enables adding new SoCs with minimal logic changes.

5) Device Tree first, no board files
- Parse DMA channels, clocks, resets, interconnects, and stream IDs from DT.
- Upstream pattern is “bindings first, driver second”.

6) Runtime PM and clock discipline
- Use pm_runtime for autosuspend/resume around active streams.
- Enable/disable core/audio clocks only in active paths.
- Remove persistent “always-on” clock behavior from downstream code.

7) Standard DMA semantics
- Use dma_slave_config + dmaengine_prep_* consistently.
- Ensure period elapsed is IRQ-driven and lock-safe.
- Align buffer constraints to DMA engine capabilities (burst/addr width/max segment).

8) Concurrency and error-path hardening
- Protect trigger/start-stop and IRQ paths with proper locking.
- Make stop/suspend idempotent.
- Upstream reviews focus heavily on unwind paths and race-free shutdown.

9) Minimize downstream policy in kernel
- Remove hardcoded use-case logic, custom mixer policy, and non-generic debug hooks.
- Keep only hardware control; leave policy to userspace/topology.

10) Incremental upstreaming sequence
- Step 1: DT bindings
- Step 2: core LPASS register/clock/reset support
- Step 3: PCM/DMA path (lpass-platform)
- Step 4: DAI links + machine integration
- Step 5: SoC-specific enablement patches
Small, reviewable series is the dominant successful pattern.

- Replace bespoke PCM ops with dmaengine helpers
- Introduce lpass_variant for all SoC differences
- Ensure full runtime PM coverage
- Validate pointer/period behavior under stress (xruns, suspend/resume)
- Upstream DT bindings before functional driver patches

Key migration patterns from lpass-apq8016 (ASoC) that are repeatedly used for Qualcomm audio upstreaming:

- Split common vs SoC-specific logic:
  Keep generic LPASS logic in common code, and move APQ8016-specific register layout/limits into a `lpass_variant` data struct. New SoCs then only add variant tables and minimal callbacks.

- Data-driven register description:
  Model register offsets, strides, IRQ/DMA channel counts, and bitfields as static metadata instead of hardcoded conditionals. This is the main scalability pattern for adding new Qualcomm parts.

- Device Tree as the hardware contract:
  Bind clocks, interrupts, memory regions, and audio interfaces through DT `compatible` + resources. Avoid board files/platform data; upstream support is DT-first.

- of_match + variant pointer handoff:
  Use `of_device_id.data` to pass SoC variant config into a single platform driver probe path. This minimizes duplicated driver code.

- Componentized ASoC registration:
  Register CPU DAI/component cleanly and let machine drivers connect topology later. Platform/IP block enablement is separated from board/audio-routing policy.

- DMA channel abstraction:
  Represent RDMA/WRDMA channel capabilities in core structures, then map per-SoC constraints via variant data. This pattern is reused across LPASS generations.

- Runtime PM and clock lifecycle correctness:
  Enable clocks only when needed, pair runtime suspend/resume with register access windows, and keep probe/remove balanced. Upstream review strongly favors this pattern.

- Error-path discipline:
  Use managed resource APIs and unwind-safe probe flow. Qualcomm audio drivers that upstream smoothly generally have clean failure handling from day one.

- Incremental upstream strategy:
  Upstream in layers: DT bindings -> base LPASS platform -> DAI enablement -> machine driver/routes -> optional codec/offload features. APQ8016 follows this staged model.

- Reuse before extension:
  New Qualcomm audio platforms should first fit into existing LPASS core abstractions; only add new hooks when hardware truly differs. This reduces review friction and long-term maintenance.

- Codec interfaces (MI2S/TDM), clocking, and external codec routing in machine drivers.
- HDMI/DisplayPort audio done in separate codec/platform pieces.
- Pattern: avoid SoC monolith; align with ASoC component model.

3) Device Tree first, board-agnostic driver behavior
- Describe clocks, power domains, interconnect paths, LPASS node, and DMA/interrupt resources in DT.
- Driver consumes DT properties, avoids board-specific hardcoding.
- Add/extend YAML bindings before/with driver changes.

4) Clock and power sequencing centralized and explicit
- Use runtime PM consistently; only enable LPASS clocks when stream starts.
- Keep clock parents/rates in DT/CC drivers; ASoC driver just votes/enables.
- Pattern: aggressive autosuspend and balanced clk_prepare/enable lifecycle for upstream acceptance.

5) Prefer regmap and field-based register descriptions
- Define SoC register regions and masks in variant tables.
- Access through regmap helpers instead of scattered readl/writel.
- Easier bring-up across SoCs with similar LPASS generations.

6) DMA model migration: LPASS-specific + generic PCM ops
- Keep LPASS DMA programming in platform DMA ops, expose standard ALSA PCM behavior.
- Capture/playback constraints (period bytes, burst, channels) encoded per-SoC in variant data.
- Pattern: standardized ALSA side, SoC-specific DMA tuning in one place.

7) DAI capability expressed declaratively
- MI2S/TDM lane count, rates, sample formats, and direction caps are declared in SoC tables.
- Avoid special-case code per stream type.
- Makes later SoC additions a capability-table extension.

8) SoundWire/WSA/VA macro integration via separate components
- Don’t fold codec macro control into LPASS CPU driver.
- Use existing codec/SDW drivers and bind via DPCM links in machine driver.
- Pattern: CPU DAI stays transport-focused; audio topology lives in card graph.

9) Interconnect/bandwidth voting added as stream lifecycle hooks
- For modern Qualcomm SoCs, add ICC votes on hw_params/prepare and release on stop.
- Keep minimal default votes and scale with use case.
- Upstream pattern: no hidden firmware assumptions; explicit kernel-side BW management.

10) Error handling and probe order designed for deferred probing
- LPASS should tolerate missing codec/clock/interconnect providers and defer cleanly.
- Use devm-managed resources and unwind paths accepted by reviewers.

11) Compatible-string evolution strategy
- Add new compatible for SoC-specific variant (e.g., sc7280-lpass) while reusing common fallback where valid.
- Keep per-SoC deltas minimal to avoid binding churn.

12) Upstream sequencing pattern
- Typical accepted order:
  a) DT bindings
  b) core/common refactors (if needed)
  c) SoC variant support (lpass-sc7280)
  d) machine driver/audio routing
  e) board DT enablement
- This reduces review friction and bisect breakage.

Practical “migration template” for next Qualcomm SoC:
- Copy nearest LPASS generation variant (e.g., sc7280/sc7180 family),
- update only register map + caps + clocks/icc,
- add DT binding + compatible,
- wire machine links for actual codecs,
- verify runtime PM/clock/icc symmetry under playback/capture suspend-resume.

Key migration patterns visible around q6afe (QDSP6 AFE) when moving Qualcomm audio code upstream:

1) Split monolith into DSP service blocks
- Downstream “audio core” logic gets separated into q6afe (front-end), q6asm (streams), q6adm (routing), q6routing, etc.
- Each block has a narrow API, making review/upstream acceptance easier.

2) Replace board-specific hardcoding with DT-driven data
- Port IDs, interface types, and routing endpoints move from machine files/static tables to device tree bindings.
- SoC differences are handled with per-compatible data tables, not ifdef-heavy code.

3) Converge to standard ASoC component/DAI model
- Legacy MSM audio hooks are rewritten as normal ASoC DAI drivers and component ops.
- Stream startup/shutdown/hw_params become standard callbacks.

4) Formalize DSP messaging path
- Ad-hoc command code is normalized through APR/GPR helper layers with common packet builders.
- Async replies/events use completions/workqueues with explicit timeout/retry/error paths.

5) Introduce capability/version tolerance
- Driver checks firmware/service version and feature bits, then selects command formats or falls back.
- Avoids tight coupling to one vendor firmware drop.

6) Push power/clock control into kernel frameworks
- Manual clock votes and hand-rolled PM are migrated to runtime PM, clk, reset, and interconnect APIs.
- Active stream state drives power transitions.

7) Convert routing to generic DAPM/ASoC controls
- Proprietary mixer/routing concepts map to kcontrols, DAPM widgets/routes, and standard ALSA semantics.
- Keeps user-space interfaces stable while internals change.

8) Improve concurrency and lifecycle handling
- Global locks get narrowed; per-port/per-stream state is tracked explicitly.
- Probe/remove/error unwind paths are made deterministic for upstream quality.

9) Minimize downstream-only abstractions
- Vendor wrappers are removed in favor of kernel primitives (regmap, clk, dmaengine, PM domains, etc.).
- Easier cross-SoC reuse and maintainer review.

10) Upstream in small, dependency-ordered patchsets
- Bindings first, then core transport, then q6afe service, then machine/card integration.
- Each patch is bisectable and testable on at least one reference platform.

Key migration patterns for q6adm (ASoC DSP ADM) in Qualcomm audio upstreaming:

1) Tight APR command code moved behind stable helpers
- Raw APR packet construction is progressively wrapped in common q6 helpers.
- Result: less duplicated packet layout logic across ADM/ASM/AFE and easier ABI maintenance.

2) Platform data -> Device Tree driven routing
- COPP/port setup, backend links, and DSP endpoint mapping are shifted to DT-described topology.
- Result: machine drivers stop hardcoding board-specific ADM routing.

3) Global state -> per-device/per-path context
- Static globals are replaced with struct-scoped state (per ADM instance, per COPP, per port).
- Result: better multi-device safety and cleaner probe/remove lifecycle.

4) Synchronous “send and hope” -> tracked async transactions
- Command completion is tied to token/port/copp IDs with wait-for-ack patterns.
- Timeouts and return-code propagation are improved.
- Result: deterministic error handling and fewer race conditions.

5) Implicit DSP assumptions -> explicit capability/config flows
- Sample rate, channels, bit width, topology ID, perf mode become explicit parameters.
- Result: clearer userspace-to-DSP contract and easier extension for new codecs/features.

6) Board-specific mixes -> reusable q6dsp service layering
- ADM responsibilities are narrowed to routing/matrix/COPP control; ASM/AFE concerns stay separated.
- Result: cleaner subsystem boundaries and easier upstream review.

7) Ad-hoc locking -> consistent lock domains
- Mutex/spinlock usage is clarified around command path vs callback path.
- Result: safer concurrent stream open/close/reconfigure operations.

8) Silent fallback paths -> strict validation
- Port IDs, app types, channel maps, and payload sizes are validated early.
- Result: fewer undefined DSP states; failures happen early with useful errno.

9) Legacy naming/IDs -> upstream-friendly enums/macros
- Downstream-style magic numbers are replaced with named constants and uapi-aligned definitions.
- Result: readable code and less drift between kernel components.

10) Calibration blobs as side effects -> explicit lifecycle hooks
- ADM setup increasingly coordinated with calibration/load events rather than hidden in start paths.
- Result: predictable sequencing for bring-up and suspend/resume.

11) Verbose ad-hoc logs -> structured debug points
- Debug output converges around command submit/ack/error points.
- Result: better diagnosability without excessive log noise.

12) Monolithic downstream drop -> incremental upstream slices
- Common pattern: first land transport/helpers, then service core, then machine integration, then controls/features.
- Result: reviewable patch sets and reduced regression risk.

Key migration patterns seen when upstreaming Qualcomm q6asm (ASM) audio support:

- Keep DSP transport and ASoC glue separate
  - q6asm handles APR message protocol/session state.
  - Front-end/back-end DAIs, routing, and machine policy stay in ASoC drivers.
  - This split is essential for reviewability and reuse across SoCs.

- Normalize legacy downstream “ASM use-cases” into generic ALSA flows
  - Map ASM sessions to ALSA PCM/compress streams.
  - Use standard hw_params/trigger/pointer semantics instead of vendor-only IOCTL paths.

- Convert static downstream assumptions into DT-driven configuration
  - No hardcoded port IDs/topology IDs in board files.
  - Use device tree for links, clocks, memory, and audio-routing.

- Make APR command handling fully asynchronous and state-driven
  - Open/configure/run/flush/close as explicit state transitions.
  - Wait for DSP ACK/event completions with timeout/error propagation.
  - Avoid synchronous “send and assume success” patterns from downstream trees.

- Rework buffer management to upstream DMA rules
  - Move from ad-hoc ION/physical assumptions to dma-mapped shared buffers.
  - Use kernel DMA APIs, proper cache sync, and clear period accounting.
  - Keep DSP-visible metadata structures version-safe and packed correctly.

- Upstream-friendly locking and lifetime management
  - Per-session locks, refcounted handles, and orderly teardown on SSR (subsystem restart).
  - Convert global mutable state into per-stream/session context.
  - Ensure callback paths are race-safe with close/free.

- Robust SSR/recovery behavior as first-class requirement
  - Detect DSP restart, invalidate stale sessions, return meaningful ALSA errors.
  - Reopen/reconfigure sessions cleanly when userspace restarts streams.

- Replace downstream logging/debug hooks with standard kernel facilities
  - dev_dbg/dev_err, tracepoints/debugfs only where justified.
  - Remove vendor-specific debug controls unless generalized.

- Upstream increment strategy
  - Land minimal playback/capture first.
  - Add compressed/offload/gapless/metadata features in follow-up patches.
  - Keep each patch focused: protocol definitions, core q6asm, then machine integration.

- Forward-looking migration trend
  - Older ASM-based paths are increasingly complemented/replaced by APM/Graph (AudioReach) on newer SoCs.
  - Reusable pattern: preserve a thin DSP service client layer and keep ASoC integration generic, so protocol backends (ASM vs APM) can evolve independently.

Key migration patterns from q6asm-dai (ASoC DSP DAI) that are useful for Qualcomm audio upstreaming:

Key migration patterns seen when upstreaming Qualcomm q6compress-dai (ASoC compress offload):

- Ensure callback paths cannot race with close/free.
- Guarantee session cleanup on all error exits.

7) Add proper runtime PM and clock voting
- Tie DSP path enable/disable to stream lifecycle.
- Avoid always-on clocks/power domains from downstream implementations.

8) Upstream-friendly control surface
- Expose only standard ALSA controls where possible.
- Push vendor-specific tuning/debug controls out of fast path (debugfs/tracepoints).

9) Error handling and unwind quality
- Use devm and structured unwind labels.
- Ensure APR/GPR handle release, memory unmap, and DSP session close always occur.

10) Incremental patching strategy (important for acceptance)
- Patch 1: common DSP helper refactor
- Patch 2: q6compress-dai conversion
- Patch 3: DT binding/schema updates
- Patch 4: machine driver wiring
- Patch 5: cleanup/removal of obsolete downstream hooks

11) SSR/restart resilience as an upstream requirement
- Re-register services after DSP restart.
- Mark streams broken and report recoverable errors instead of hanging userspace.

12) Keep ABI and userspace behavior stable
- Preserve tinycompress expectations (fragment accounting, pointer behavior, drain semantics).
- Validate with standard compress-offload playback/regression tests.

Key migration patterns seen around q6routing (QDSP6 ASoC DSP routing) when moving Qualcomm audio code upstream:

1) Control-path decoupling
- Legacy: routing logic tightly coupled to APR packet building and DSP service IDs.
- Upstream pattern: keep APR/GLINK transport in lower layers (q6adm/q6apm/etc.), expose clean ASoC component ops in routing code.

2) Hardcoded route tables -> declarative topology
- Legacy: static C arrays for FE/BE/port mappings, often board-specific.

- Legacy: direct use of ASM/ADM port/session numeric IDs in mixer controls.
- Upstream: map IDs to ALSA-facing DAIs/controls; hide DSP-internal IDs behind helper translation layers.

- Legacy: one large machine file handling backend selection, clocks, and DSP setup.
- Upstream: split into codec/platform/machine responsibilities; q6routing handles only route state and DSP matrix programming.

- Upstream: SOC_ENUM_EXT/SOC_SINGLE_EXT style controls with explicit get/put callbacks, bounded values, and stable userspace ABI.

6) Ad-hoc lifecycle handling -> runtime PM + refcounted paths
- Legacy: manual start/stop ordering and fragile enable/disable sequences.
- Upstream: route enable/disable tied to stream lifecycle, DAPM events, runtime PM, and reference counting for shared backends.

7) Async DSP events normalized
- Legacy: command completion handling embedded in route code.
- Upstream: centralize async completion/error paths; route code waits on generic completion primitives and propagates Linux error codes.

8) Board quirks isolated
- Legacy: route code includes device-specific conditionals.
- Upstream: quirks moved to DT flags, match data, or tiny per-SoC hooks; common routing core remains reusable.

9) Validation and locking tightened
- Legacy: weak checks on FE/BE state and port reuse.
- Upstream: strict parameter validation, mutex-protected route state, and deterministic teardown to avoid stale matrix entries.

10) Naming/API convergence
- Legacy: downstream naming (COPP/POP/AFE paths) exposed directly.
- Upstream: align with upstream ASoC naming (DAI links, widgets, PCM paths), minimizing downstream-only concepts in public interfaces.

6) Incremental enablement strategy

- Then add AFE/ASM/ADM functionality in small reviewable patches.

Pattern: smallest working audio path before advanced use-cases.

- Map backend/frontend DAIs to standard DPCM flows.

Pattern: ALSA topology drives routing, DSP services provide execution.

8) Resource and power-domain integration

9) ABI caution with firmware interfaces
- Keep command IDs/version handling backward compatible.

10) Logging and observability uplift
- Replace noisy prints with dev_dbg/dev_err, ratelimited paths.

Pattern: maintainable diagnostics acceptable to upstream review.

11) Common-code extraction across Qualcomm families
- Merge repeated qdsp6 helpers into shared modules.
- Keep LPASS/SoC machine differences in thin wrappers.
Pattern: maximize reuse, minimize duplicate downstream carry.

12) Review-oriented coding style changes
- Kernel-doc, SPDX, YAML bindings, strict dtbs_check compliance.
- Smaller patches grouped by subsystem ownership (ASoC, remoteproc, DT).
Pattern: technical correctness plus process compatibility for upstream acceptance.

Key migration patterns visible from apq8016-sbc (and generally useful for Qualcomm ASoC upstreaming):

1) Board logic moves to DT, not C
- Machine driver keeps policy thin.
- Card model, routing, and endpoint wiring are described in Device Tree (audio-routing, dai phandles), reducing hardcoded board data.

2) Use standard ASoC card model, avoid vendor audio frameworks
- Upstream path uses snd_soc_card / snd_soc_dai_link / DAPM instead of downstream Qualcomm-only abstractions.
- Keeps integration aligned with common ALSA SoC flows.

3) Split complex codec blocks into independent components
- Qualcomm WCD paths are handled as separate digital/analog pieces and linked through normal DAI/component registration.
- This mirrors hardware partitioning and improves reuse across boards.

4) Keep machine driver “glue-only”
- apq8016-sbc primarily binds CPU DAI(s), codec DAI(s), routes, and controls clocks/pinctrl.
- Codec-specific behavior stays in codec drivers; LPASS specifics stay in platform/CPU DAI drivers.

5) Prefer runtime-managed resources
- Clocks, pinctrl, and power sequencing are handled with runtime PM and ASoC startup/shutdown hooks, not always-on board init.
- Reduces power and matches upstream lifecycle expectations.

6) Express audio paths with DAPM routes/widgets
- Speaker, mic, headset paths are represented as DAPM graph entries.
- Enables automatic power gating and avoids custom power toggling code.

7) Follow FE/BE and link naming conventions where applicable
- Frontend/backends and clear DAI link naming make topology maintainable and easier to review upstream.
- Reduces board-specific special-casing.

8) Replace downstream GPIO/jack hacks with standard jack/reporting APIs
- Jack detection and button reporting are integrated via codec/component mechanisms and ALSA jack APIs.
- Avoids ad-hoc input plumbing.

9) Minimize platform conditionals in machine file
- One driver supports a family/board via DT matching and small quirks, rather than per-product forks.
- This is a major upstream acceptance pattern for Qualcomm audio.

10) Upstream incrementally: LPASS + codec + machine, then refine
- First land basic playback/capture links.
- Then add routing completeness, jack, power optimizations, and optional interfaces (additional MI2S/SLIMbus paths).
